notes:
I've built verse-by-verse notes from the pages I could read. Some gaps to know about first:

- **Missing traditions:** I found nothing from the Methodist/Wesleyan sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) or the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) on this chapter. Luther shows up only second-hand, in one line of the Pulpit Commentary.
- **No prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching** on this chapter turned up.
- **Not consulted:** the netbible.org notes directly (only one NET note quoted on Precept Austin), Ellicott beyond a single line, and Guzik's notes on vv. 12–13 (my copy cut off at v. 11).
- **Precept Austin:** the page I read only goes as far as v. 1. Its comments on later verses come from search snippets.

Some pages came back as plain text that can't be cited line by line (Guzik/Enduring Word, the Pulpit Commentary and the main Precept Austin page). For those I've summarised and given the URL only.

---

## Background: how the chapter is read

- **Two levels.** Most Christian and Jewish readers took the Song as an allegory, Christians from at least Origen in the 3rd century. The allegorical reading dominated until the 19th century; modern scholarship then pushed toward the literal sense, and many commentators now read the Song only as married love. Kyle Dillon at The Gospel Coalition argues for both: the Song is an allegory of Christ and the church "because marriage itself is designed as an allegory of Christ and the church." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/song-songs-sex-or-jesus/
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey).** Christian reading since Hippolytus and Origen has two strands. One is about the church (Christ and his church); the other is about the individual soul with Christ as bridegroom. https://voice.bibleodyssey.org/articles/jewish-and-christian-interpretation-of-the-song-of-songs/
- **Catholic.** The old Catholic Encyclopedia says "most Catholics accept the allegorical interpretation." It adds that "in the Breviary and Missal the Church has repeatedly applied the song to the Mother of God." https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/canticle-of-canticles
  - A Catholic Answers magazine article reads the book as celebrating the renewed covenant between Yahweh and the "remnant" of Israel back from exile in Babylon. It cites a view in which the shepherdess rejects the king's approaches and is content with simple rural life. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/song-of-songs
- **Orthodox.** Fr. Lawrence Farley says the Fathers took the historical meaning as given and treated the allegorical as more important, but he suggests the historical level now has a new importance. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/reading-the-song-of-solomon-today
- **Where the chapter sits.** Precept Austin uses Swindoll's outline: 7:1–8:14 is "The Marriage Deepens," with the Song as a foreshadowing of Christ and the church. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7

---

## v. 1

- **Who is speaking?** Teachers really disagree here.
  - MacArthur (Baptist; gty.org study Bible) thinks vv. 1–5 are spoken by the friends, not Solomon. Carr agrees and gives the man only vv. 6–9. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7
  - The Pulpit Commentary also assigns vv. 1–5 to the court ladies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
  - Criswell treats vv. 1–9 as Solomon's third description of his wife. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7
- **Dance?** Guzik says the feet-to-head order suggests she is dancing. He finds no biblical evidence of provocative public dancing, so he thinks it is either just a poetic image or a private display for her husband. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
- **"Prince's daughter."**
  - Carr: the phrase is about her noble character, not royal birth. MacArthur: she looked royal but came from a humble background. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the Hebrew means "noble in disposition." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- **Sandals.** The NET note says aristocratic women wore sandals while lower-class women usually went barefoot. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7
- **Thighs.** Carr says the word means the upper thigh, and the dance shows its symmetrical beauty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7
  - Adam Clarke instead thinks the "joints" mean ornaments on the clothing worn by Eastern ladies. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/7-1.html
- **Allegorical readings.**
  - Pulpit's sermon section links the beautiful feet to Isaiah 52:7 and the church's missionary work. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
  - JFB: a princely bride freely gives the word of life to others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/song-of-solomon-7.html
  - Everett: the believer as a child of the King. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 2

- **Literal readings.**
  - Guzik quotes Glickman: wine and wheat were the basic foods of a meal, so her body is a feast to him. Guzik doubts the "lilies" point to anything sexually explicit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
  - Constable says the Hebrew word for "navel" may refer to one of her private parts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/7-1.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls the description chaste. It explains the heap of wheat from village threshing floors and says not every detail should get a symbolic meaning. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- **Allegorical readings.**
  - The Puritan John Trapp (quoted by Guzik) made the navel baptism and the wheat the Lord's Supper. Guzik uses this as an example of how hard allegory becomes here. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
  - JFB translates "navel" as "girdle-clasp" and stresses that she is clothed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/song-of-solomon-7.html
  - Kingcomments: the round goblet with no beginning or end is a picture of the new, eternal life we have been given. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 3

- Guzik: the picture repeats 4:5 and suggests innocence, attractiveness and matching form. Trapp read the two breasts as the two Testaments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
- JFB reads the twin fawns as faith and love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 4

- **Neck.** Guzik: an ivory tower suggests nobility and strength, not length. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
- **Pools of Heshbon.** The Pulpit Commentary says the eyes glisten like still water. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
  - Kingcomments (allegorical): her eyes radiate the peace of God's Word. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/song-of-solomon-7.html
- **Nose / tower of Lebanon.** Carr (via Guzik): "Lebanon" comes from a root meaning "white," so the compliment is about her fair colouring, not size. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
  - JFB (allegorical): the nose stands for spiritual discernment, such as ministers guarding against danger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 5

- **Literal.** The Pulpit Commentary says Carmel shows how well her head sits on her neck. "Purple" hair is black hair catching the light, and the onlookers see the king captivated. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
  - Carr (via Guzik): "tresses" means hair that ripples like running water. Glickman: the wedding night had sevenfold praise, this has tenfold, so their love has deepened. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
- **Allegorical.** JFB makes the "galleries" where the King is held the ordinances and means of grace, where Christ and believers meet. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/song-of-solomon-7.html
- **Charismatic.** Everett cites Mike Bickle (a charismatic teacher): v. 5 is about believers whose sacrifice and devotion have "held the Lord captive", so their prayers may move God to act. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 6

- Guzik: here the husband himself is clearly speaking. He applies the verse to God's delight in his people (Isaiah 62:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
- Pulpit: "love" means "loved one," and he delights that she is his own. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- Matthew Henry: the church is "made fair," not born that way, but given beauty by Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/7-1.html
- Ibn Ezra (quoted via Precept Austin): nothing in the world is as fair and pleasant as love. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7

## v. 7

- Ellicott: the clusters are probably dates; the word "grapes" was added in English to match v. 8. Benson: the palm is upright and stays green under pressure. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/7-7.htm
- Gill (allegorical): the church's stature is "the stature of the fulness of Christ" (Ephesians 4:13). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/7-7.htm
- Guzik: the palm tree speaks of her character and bearing, not just her looks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the palm and vine are both used for God's people (Psalm 92:12; John 15). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 8

- **Literal.** Guzik: the husband rightly wants married lovemaking (compare Proverbs 5:18–20), and their love has matured. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
  - Everett: many Christian scholars read vv. 6–9 as a description of sexual intercourse. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/song-of-solomon-7.html
- **Spiritual.** Everett: climbing the palm means the Lord releasing his anointing through his servant. Watchman Nee read the fragrant breath as the fragrance of Christ. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/song-of-solomon-7.html
- Pulpit's sermon section: the Lord delights in the "fruits of righteousness" of his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 9

- **Hard text.** The Pulpit Commentary says the verse cannot be translated with certainty and lists several old versions. Luther took it as wine that "speaks of the previous year." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- **Speaker.** The Bible Knowledge Commentary has her break in mid-verse. Their intertwined voices mirror their kisses, and the rare word *dabab* ("flowing gently") is hard to pin down. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7
  - The Pulpit Commentary disagrees and keeps the king speaking until v. 10. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- Guzik (quoting Glickman): a picture of the couple falling asleep, with sex here nourishing the marriage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/

## v. 10

This is the key verse, and the views differ most here.

- **Genesis 3:16.** Several older writers link "desire" to the curse on the woman.
  - Adam Clarke (Methodist): the same word is used in Genesis 3:16, so the curse seems to be reversed: now his desire is toward her. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/7-10.html
  - Matthew Poole: her desire toward him is her duty under Genesis 3:16, but his desire toward her is wonderful condescension. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/7-10.htm
  - Keil and Delitzsch also see a link to Genesis 3:16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/7-10.htm
  - The Bible Hub study note sees a reversal and restoration of relational harmony. https://biblehub.com/songs/7-10.htm
- **Growing security.** Deere notes she no longer says "my beloved is mine," only that his desire is for her, a sign of how secure she has become. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7
  - Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: this is complete abandonment, together with knowing the beloved is satisfied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
- **Reformed and Baptist readings about Christ.**
  - Gill: the church's assurance of union with Christ. Christ's desire was toward her "from everlasting" and led him to the cross. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/7-10.htm
  - Matthew Henry: the believing soul glories that she belongs to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/7-10.html
  - Desiring God: we can say "I am my beloved's" *now*, not once we are holy enough. "Right now I belong to Jesus as much as I ever will." https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/his-desire-is-for-me
- **The "shepherd" reading (a minority view).** Here the Shulamite turns *down* Solomon and stays loyal to a shepherd lover.
  - Cambridge Bible: "the bride openly rejects the king." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/7-10.htm
  - Coffman (Church of Christ) argues "his" cannot mean Solomon: "He was the shepherd, not the king." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/7-10.html
  - The Pulpit's v. 10 note mentions this view too, but its main notes on vv. 1–9 assume the speaker is her husband. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 11

- **Literal.** Guzik: she now invites him, echoing his invitation in 2:10. It shows she has grown in confidence and that the woman can also take the lead toward intimacy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
  - Pulpit: she prefers the country to the court. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- **Allegorical.** JFB links the "villages" to the scattering and preaching of Acts 8. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/song-of-solomon-7.html
  - Kingcomments: going to the fields means going to work for the harvest, as the bride leaves her 'comfort zone'. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/song-of-solomon-7.html

## v. 12

- Pulpit: springtime, and "my love" means expressions of her love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- Matthew Henry: "There will I give thee my love" is the church promising Christ her "best affections." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/7-10.html
- Pulpit's sermon section: Christ gives his love tokens "in the field of service." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- TGC's commentary: she finds the right time and place, the secluded vineyards, to give the pleasures she has "laid up" for him. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/

## v. 13

- Pulpit: mandrakes were "love flowers," used as an aphrodisiac (compare Genesis 30:14). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/song-of-solomon-7.html
- Bible Hub study notes: the treasures she has stored up show the depth and richness of their relationship. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/songs/7.htm
- One devotional writer on Precept Austin connects "new and old" to love saved for marriage: "True love is worth waiting for." https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_7
- Kingcomments (allegorical): the "fresh and old fruits" show a bride freed from her self-centeredness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/song-of-solomon-7.html
